title: Teach It To Learn It
goal: Your kid takes something they already know how to do, a card trick, a soccer move, a recipe, a drawing, and teaches it to someone else in a real, planned lesson. They break it into steps, find the tricky part, teach it, and check that their student can actually do it.
need: A skill your kid already knows well, and whatever props it needs
A student: you, a sibling, a friend or a grandparent

lesson.text: A good lesson isn't just explaining. You show it, let the learner try with help, then step back and check. Four moves: show, explain, try together, check.
lesson.before: Okay, you just do this, then this, see? Easy. Got it?

model.line: Watch me make one pupusa, start to finish.
Roll a ball, press a hole with your thumb, add cheese, close it, then pat it flat. Gently, or the cheese leaks out.
Your turn. I'll help you with the patting.
Now make one on your own, and I won't say anything.

lesson.modelNote: Asking 'got it?' checks nothing. The fix ends with the student making one alone, teacher silent, and that's when you see what landed.

academics.subject: Speaking
academics.text: explaining clearly, choosing the right words, and holding someone's attention

academics.subject: Thinking
academics.text: breaking a whole skill into ordered steps, and spotting the hardest one

academics.subject: Writing
academics.text: a simple plan and a step-by-step card for the student

academics.subject: Life skills
academics.text: patience, reading someone's confusion, and adjusting on the fly

howTo.intro: Be a real beginner: try with your hands, get stuck where a beginner would, and say so out loud. At the check, stay silent and let them stay silent too. That's when you both see what the lesson actually taught.

plan.what: The terrible lesson, then pick the skill and break it down (Steps 1 and 2). 20 minutes.
Plan the lesson and make one helper card (Step 3). 20 minutes.

plan.when: Same day or the day after
plan.what: Teach it, check it, fix it and teach again (Steps 4 and 5). 30 minutes.

troubleshoot.q: They can't explain a step they do automatically
troubleshoot.a: Don't rescue them. Ask them to do it very slowly while you watch, and name each move out loud. That struggle is the understanding forming.

troubleshoot.q: They get frustrated when you don't get it
troubleshoot.a: Remind them it's the lesson being tested, not you or them. Then ask: what could you show me differently?

troubleshoot.q: A sibling student won't take it seriously
troubleshoot.a: Keep it under 10 minutes and let the sibling choose which skill they want to learn. Or you play student first, and the sibling gets the improved lesson in Step 5.

fromHome.text: Pupusas were our favourite meal in El Salvador, so we tried making them at home, and my son taught his sister how.

skills.name: Explaining
skills.text: turning something automatic into clear steps

skills.name: Structuring
skills.text: breaking a skill into an order that builds

skills.name: Confidence

steps.title: Watch a terrible lesson
steps.why: You teach them something badly on purpose, then they pick their own skill.
steps.kid: First, your kid watches you teach them something simple in the worst way possible: you mumble, skip steps, rush and never let them try. They spot everything that went wrong. Then they choose a skill they know really well, small enough to teach in one sitting.
steps.you: Teach something small, like a paper plane, and ham it up: 'You just fold it, then, you know, do the thing. Done!' Then ask what would have made it a good lesson. Help them pick a skill, and steer away from anything too big for one sitting.
starters: A few words in another language
ask: What made my lesson so bad?
What do you know how to do that you could teach me?
steps.tip: The best skill to teach is one they already love. Their enthusiasm is half of a good lesson.

levels.explore: Say 2 things that were wrong with the bad lesson, then pick a simple, familiar skill.
levels.develop: List what a good lesson needs, then pick a skill with at least 4 steps.
levels.extend: Pick a skill you do without thinking, and guess which step you'll forget to teach.

steps.title: Break it down and find the tricky bit
steps.why: Your kid turns the skill into clear steps and spots where beginners get stuck.
steps.kid: Your kid does the skill very slowly and writes each move as a step, in order: 'first you cross the laces, then you make a loop.' They'll skip tiny automatic moves at first, and finding those is the discovery. Then they circle the step where beginners get stuck and plan how to explain it.
steps.you: Keep asking 'what do you do first? and then?' Play the confused beginner to help them find the tricky part: 'Wait, how did your fingers do that?'
ask: What do you do that you almost didn't notice?
Which step will be hardest for me?
steps.tip: The step they forgot to write down is exactly the one a beginner needs most.

levels.explore: Draw the 3 biggest steps in order and point to the hardest.
levels.develop: Write every step in order, even the tiny automatic ones, and plan the tricky one.
levels.extend: Find the step that has to come before the tricky one, and check your student can do that step first.

steps.title: Plan the lesson
steps.why: Your kid builds a lesson using the four moves, and makes one helper.
steps.kid: Your kid plans the lesson like the pupusa example: a hook to make the student want to learn (a quick demo, or why it's cool), then show, explain the steps, try together and check. They make one thing to help: a step-by-step card, a drawing, or a slow demo version.
steps.you: Read their plan as the student would, and ask the two questions every student wants answered: how will you start so I want to learn? When do I get to try it myself?
ask: How will you start so I actually want to learn this?
Would a picture or a card make a step clearer?
steps.tip: The best lessons aren't lectures, they're do-alongs. Make sure the plan has the student's hands busy, not just their ears.

levels.explore: Plan 3 boxes: show, steps, their try.
levels.develop: Add a hook, a try-together moment, and one helper card.
levels.extend: Write what your student must do alone at the end first, then plan backwards from that check.

steps.title: Teach it for real
steps.why: The lesson itself, and the test at the end: can the student do it alone?
steps.kid: Your kid teaches the lesson following their plan: hook, show, explain, try together. When the student gets stuck, they think on their feet: rephrase, show it again, find another way to say it. At the end, they check: can the student now do the skill on their own, without help?
steps.you: Be a genuine, willing learner. Get it wrong where a beginner would, and say what confused you. At the check, give an honest attempt. Success or fail, it's a clue about the teaching, not a score on anyone.
ask: How else could you explain that step?
Can your student do it on their own now?
steps.tip: Watching your kid rephrase on the fly when you're stuck is the best part. That second explanation is where the teaching happens.

levels.explore: Teach the skill start to finish and watch the student try it alone.
levels.develop: Guide the student through a try, then check whether they learned the whole skill.
levels.extend: When they get stuck, show it a different way, not the same words louder, and note which way worked.

steps.title: Teach it better
steps.why: Your kid fixes what didn't land, teaches again, and looks back.
steps.kid: Looking at where the student struggled, your kid revises the lesson: a clearer explanation for the tricky bit, a missing step, a better order. Then they teach it again, to the same person or someone new. Finally, they think about what teaching taught them about the skill itself.
steps.you: Point to the moment you got confused, kindly and specifically. Praise the teaching, not just the skill: 'That second explanation really helped me get it' means more than 'good job.'
ask: What's the one change that made the lesson clearer?
Do you understand the skill better now than before you taught it?
steps.tip: Change one thing between lessons, not everything. Then you both know which change made the difference.

levels.explore: Name one thing to improve and try the lesson again.
levels.develop: Fix the weak part of the lesson and teach it again.
levels.extend: Check your student again a day later, with no reminder. What did they keep, and what does that say about your lesson?

conclusion.headline: Their student can do it alone now.
conclusion.text: Say you want to learn their skill too, then do one step wrong on purpose. They should spot it, name the step, and know how to explain it better the second time.
conclusion.celebrate: The first time their student does it alone, say quietly: 'You didn't touch it once. They did that because of how you taught it.'
extensions: Teach the same skill to a younger kid and see how the lesson has to change
Run a family skill swap where everyone teaches everyone one thing
Teach something harder next, with more steps
Film the lesson as a real how-to video

signs: They explain things in steps instead of 'just do it like this'
They notice when someone is confused and try another way
They offer to teach things to younger kids or visitors
makeItReal: Teach someone who genuinely wants the skill: a grandparent learning a card trick over video, a younger cousin learning to ride, a friend who's always wanted to braid. Let your kid set the time, run the lesson and do the final check.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

onTheRoad: Learn a game from local kids at a playground, with you nearby, then teach it to your family that evening.
Teach a quick trick to a kid who doesn't speak your language, with you close by, using only showing and trying together.
Ask a local, with your help, to teach you a small skill, and notice which teaching moves they use.
backHome: Teach one skill you learned on the road to a friend at home, and tell them where you learned it.

classroom.intro: With a class, students teach each other: half the room teaches while the other half learns, then they switch. Everyone gets to be both teacher and student, and the final check shows what each lesson really taught.

tips.d: Open with Step 1 for the whole class: teach a paper plane the worst way possible. Students list everything that went wrong, and that list becomes their checklist.
Pair students who know different skills. In round one, A teaches B, then B teaches A. For Step 5, each teacher finds a new student.
Steer students to skills with small props: a card trick, a paper fold, a drawing, a bracelet knot, a few words in another language. Skip anything needing a stove or a field.
The learner takes the parent's job: try with their hands, get stuck honestly, say out loud what confused them, and stay quiet at the final check.
Explore kids plan three boxes: show, steps, their try. Develop kids add a hook and a helper card. Extend kids write the final check first and plan backwards.
Finish by having students teach their skill to a younger buddy class. It's the most real audience a school has, and little kids ask the honest questions.

classroom.timing: Plan three sessions of about 45 minutes: the terrible lesson and breaking skills down, planning and helper cards, then teaching, checking and reteaching. A buddy class visit can be a fourth. At home, kids teach the skill to someone in the family.
